papers.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
f: Section 7.3 'Locked versus long', p. 6; Table 9, p. 17

Loops that run to the length limit are set mostly by temperature, not by top-p: of 360 structured-output generations (3,000-token limit, llama.cpp), Qwen3-4B loops to the limit in 59 with the default sampler (T 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20), 53 at T 0.6 with no truncation, and 24 at T 1 with no truncation; Llama-3.1-8B 54, 40 and 0. Removing top-p at T 0.6 removes only 6 of 59 and 14 of 54 limit loops. Prompts are structured output (JSON, tables, lists), not math reasoning.
At τ = 0.6 with no truncation nothing locks, yet 53 (Qwen3-4B) and 40 (Llama-3.1-8B) of 360 structured generations loop to the limit, against 59 and 54 with the default sampler (24 and 0 at τ = 1)
Abstract; Theorem 1 and Proposition 3, p. 3; Table 2, p. 7

Mechanism: under top-p with threshold pi, a loop position becomes deterministic (escape probability exactly 0) once the raw probability q of the loop token reaches pi; with temperature applied before top-p (transformers order) at T 0.7 and top-p 0.9 the sufficient threshold falls from q >= 0.9 to q >= 0.823. Teacher-forced on 150 repeated units per model, 11 models: 71%-100% of units stay locked under top-p 0.9, 0% under pure sampling (Table 2). Pure sampling still leaves a per-repetition escape probability of 10^-1.5 to 10^-3.5 (Appendix B), so loops can still reach a token limit.
Pure sampling never locks; top-p with threshold π > 1/2 locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches π
Appendix G, Table 16, p. 19-20

A count-based repetition penalty (penalty grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences of a 24-token context, a'=24, c0=2, bc=3; llama.cpp patch) keeps MATH-500 accuracy at the default sampler's level: Qwen3-4B 83.2% vs 83.0% default (difference +0.2 points, 95% CI [-2.2, 2.6], n=500, one sample, 8,192-token limit), Llama-3.1-8B 49.2% vs 50.2%, and no benchmark generation loops to the limit. So on these two models removing verbatim loops by a penalty adds no MATH-500 accuracy.
With the length term re- moved, accuracy returns to the default level on all four benchmark rows, and no benchmark genera- tion loops to the limit
Appendix G, Table 16, p. 19-20

The standard DRY repetition penalty (lambda 0.8, base 1.75, allowed length 2) lowers MATH-500 accuracy: Qwen3-4B 83.0% -> 68.8% (-14.2 points, 95% CI [-18.0, -10.4], n=500), Llama-3.1-8B 50.2% -> 38.8% (-11.4 points); GSM8K -2.5 and -5.1 points. Cause: its length term penalizes any verbatim match of 3+ tokens and derivations reuse expressions. Do not use DRY or n-gram blocking as the loop fix for math reasoning.
On Qwen MATH- 500, 58 of the 85 problems that DRY loses hit the token limit
Section 5, Table 1, p. 4; Section 7.3 and Table 2, p. 6-7

Bounded penalties do not release a locked loop under top-p 0.9: presence penalty 1.0 leaves 77%-100% of units locked and a 64-token-window frequency penalty 0.5 leaves 56%-99% locked in 10 of 11 models; min-p 0.1 locks 85%-100% of units. Only penalties that grow along the loop (full-context frequency penalty, DRY without breakers, the count term) leave 0-2% locked.
presence penalties and windowed frequency penalties come with no such guarantee

papers.title: Wait, Wait, Wait... Why Do Reasoning Models Loop?
f: Section 2, p. 3-4; Appendix A, Figure 6 and Table 1, p. 17-19

Loop fraction under greedy decoding on AIME 2024+2025 (60 problems, 20 samples per problem and temperature, 30K max tokens, each model's default top-k and top-p, no repetition penalty; loop = some 30-gram appears at least 20 times): R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B 0.76, 7B 0.49, 32B 0.37; OpenThinker3-1.5B 0.30, 7B 0.10, QwQ-32B 0.04; R1-Distill-Llama-8B 0.54; Phi-4-reasoning 0.43; Phi-4-reasoning-plus 0.45. Looping falls as temperature rises from 0 to 1.0 for every model (figures only, no table by temperature). Only temperature is varied; top-p is never varied.
All open reasoning models we tested loop at low temperature, and looping decreases as temperature increases
Appendix A.1 'Effect of RL training' and Figure 6, p. 17

RL post-training did not remove looping in the one pair tested: Phi-4-reasoning (distilled) loops in 0.43 of greedy AIME responses and Phi-4-reasoning-plus (lightly RL-tuned) in 0.45 (AIME 2024+2025, 20 samples per problem). This is evidence against 'RL on reasoning mainly removes loops' for a model that was RL-tuned after distillation; it does not cover RL from a base model (RL-Zero).
In this setting, we observe that the looping counts remain roughly the same across the two models
Section 2, p. 4; Appendix A.2, Figure 11, p. 19

Loops concentrate on hard problems: on the 20 hardest vs 20 easiest AIME problems (ranked by accuracy at T 0.8), greedy looping is 51% vs 13% for OpenThinker3-1.5B, 0.97 vs 0.33 for R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, 0.89 vs 0.03 for R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. So removing loops on hard problems need not yield correct answers: the loop marks problems the model already fails at T 0.8.
Looping at temperature 0 is then significantly higher on hard than easy problems (e.g., 51% vs. 13% for OpenThinker-3 1.5B)
Appendix B.1, p. 23

At the onset of a loop the weaker model puts little probability on a progress-making step even at T 1: continuing OpenThinker3-1.5B's own loop prefix (AIME 2025 I-7), 1/50 (T 0.7) and 8/50 (T 1.0) student continuations of 2,000 tokens contain a key insight, against 34/50 and 32/50 for the teacher QwQ-32B from the same prefix. Sampling from the loop prefix (backtrack-and-resample) is therefore a weak fix for the student; a full restart or a stronger continuation model is what changes the outcome.
At temperature 0.7, GPT-5 marks 1/50 student continuations and 34/50 teacher continuations as containing an insight (at temperature 1, these numbers are 8/50 and 32/50)
Section 1, p. 2-3; Section 3.3, p. 8; Figure 1

Temperature removes loops but not the cause: at high temperature the distilled students (OpenThinker3-1.5B/7B) still generate longer responses than the teacher QwQ-32B (Figure 1, about 14k-20k tokens axis), and in the synthetic graph task the trained model at T 1 has mean response length 67.4 vs 24.6 for a perfect learner and 72.25% accuracy at the same token budget. For an equal-token comparison this means a base model at T 1.0 spends more tokens per solved problem than a better-trained model even with no loops.
While increasing temperature largely removes looping, the student models still produce substantially longer responses than the teacher at high temperatures
Sec. 3 and Prop. 3.1, pp. 1, 5

Pipis et al. loop mechanism 1 (risk aversion): at a hard decision point the model spreads the progress action's mass over n confusable options ((1-p)/n each) while an easy cyclic action keeps mass p; greedy/low T then picks the cyclic action. Loops are seeded at HIGH-entropy decision points (star-graph root), not at confident positions.
the model puts relatively more probability on the cyclic action and gets stuck
Sec. 5 and Appendix F, Fig. 16, p. 30

Catalyst: once a loop starts, top-1 probability rises toward 1 (OpenThinker3-1.5B, greedy, AIME 2025 I-5 and I-7). So inside an established loop positions are low-entropy; a rule that sharpens low-entropy positions would reinforce a loop once begun, while onset happens at uncertain positions. Implication for entropy-split temperature: measure entropy at loop onset, not averaged over the loop.
once the loop starts, the top-1 probability rises toward

Temperature as fix: on G(5,5) with exploration, T=1 gives response length 108.1 vs 24.4 for a perfect learner (4.4x) and about 58% accuracy vs near-perfect for the teacher. Authors call temperature a stopgap. They propose only training-time fixes (margin-biased traces, hints at high-loss positions); no decoding rule that removes loops while keeping low-T accuracy is tested.
the learned model has average response length
Sec. 2, p. 2-4; Appendix A, p. 17

Loop metric: a 30-gram appearing >= 20 times; 20 samples per (problem, model, T), T in 0-1.0 step 0.2, AIME 24/25, 30K max tokens, default top-k/top-p. T=0 loop rates: R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B 76%, 32B 37%; OpenThinker3-1.5B 30% vs teacher QwQ-32B 4%. In these reasoning models accuracy rises with T, unlike our base-model case where finished answers are more accurate at T 0.6. RL-tuned Phi-4-reasoning-plus loops about as much as Phi-4-reasoning.
We do not use any repetition penalty as we focus on the role of temperature

Mechanism 2 (temporally correlated errors): at near-uniform decision points the model's small preference errors persist across revisits (top child same on 98.7% of consecutive root visits, second child 72.8%), so low T repeats the same branch. Again the loop seed is a high-entropy branch point. Only inference-time mitigation mentioned is repetition penalty, not tested.
inference-time repetition penalties pursue a related goal

J++ Lens algorithm: per layer, k-means (E=8 clusters, on 64-dim PCA of unit-normalised centred residuals, fitted on 1,000 WikiText-103 sequences) partitions source activations; one averaged Jacobian d h_final,t / d h_l,s (LRP backward pass: LN-rule on norms, identity+half rules on gated MLPs, plain gradient through attention) is fitted per cluster; the 8 expert Jacobians are summed with learned signed weights (Adam, lr 0.05, fitted on a small labelled dev set of latent-variable-extraction items); readout = top-k of W_U J_l h over the vocabulary minus tokens with no letter or digit. papers.title: Drift-Resilient TabPFN: In-Context Learning Temporal Distribution Shifts on Tabular Data
f: Sec 3.1-3.2, Algorithm 1

Domain prior = the TabPFN structural-causal-model prior (random graph, each node a weighted sum of parents + noise through a random activation) with drift added: a sparse subset of causal edges is selected, and a second randomly sampled SCM (2nd-order SCM) takes the time index c_k and outputs the weight shift of each selected edge in one forward pass, giving non-linear, correlated shifts over time. Time domains and their sample counts are sampled, with gaps. The time index enters the model through Time2Vec (1 linear + sinusoid terms). The authors call the prior heuristic, not the true dynamics. For us: structural drift is expressed as time-varying parameters of the generator, the same form as a simulator with entry/exit and repricing regimes.
modeling the dynamic of edge shifts using a 2nd-order SCM. This 2nd-order SCM is itself an SCM
Sec 4 TabPFN Setup; App A.3

Cost: 30 epochs = 30,720,000 synthetic datasets, about 7 days on 8 RTX 2080 Ti (64 CPUs, 500 GB RAM); plain TabPFN retrained the same way took 8 days. Prior hyperparameters tuned with about 40 configurations (1 day each on 4 GPUs) on 12 validation datasets; preprocessing tuned over 300 configurations. Inference 10.9 s per dataset on average. Parameter and layer counts are not stated in the paper, and no smaller configuration is reported, so this paper gives no evidence on the smallest size that works; LC-PFN (arxiv-2310.20447) does. Output is a class distribution trained with cross entropy (regression targets are discretised into classes); no bar distribution, no quantiles.

Why loops start. Statement loops follow a reasoning impasse: the model cannot solve the problem, writes a self-correction ('I think I cannot solve it. But maybe I can try'), then retries with a high density of 'Wait', 'But', 'Alternatively' sentence starts. Density and attention share of these tokens peak in the window before onset (50 loop vs 50 non-loop samples, DS-Qwen-14B). Numerical loops come from tasks needing long periodic digit expansions that fill the recent context. Both are triggered by the task, so hard problems the model cannot solve are the likely loop prompts.

Sec 3.1 Fig 3-4 (p4); Sec 3.3 Fig 8 (p6-7), DS-Qwen-14B and Qwen3-8B

Onset signature in the output distribution: at loop onset the max token probability jumps toward 1 and entropy drops toward 0 (shown as example traces, not a measured detector). Hidden states of the repeated token reach cosine similarity near 1.0 across cycles. Persistence: attention concentrates on the first tokens and the last 128 tokens, so once the recent context is repetitive the repetition is reinforced; the loop is nearly inescapable. Implication: a per-token entropy or top-1 probability monitor is a cheap onset signal; no false-positive rate is reported for it.

f: Section 3.3, Table 1, p. 5

Zeroing the output of at most 3 attention heads (no fine-tuning) raised held-out accuracy in all 12 model-task pairs: SmolLM3-3B, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on Arithmetic (1,000 test), BoolQ (3,270), HellaSwag (10,042), MBPP (500). For example, the SmolLM3 Arithmetic intervention raises accuracy from 70.40% to 83.50%, a gain of 13.10 percentage points.
Section 5 Discussion and Limitations, p. 9

Stated limitations of the head-ablation result: no claim that beneficial ablations exist for every model-task pair; selection screens single heads first so it can miss jointly beneficial sets; gains depend on the discovery data and candidate pool; an unsuccessful search would not show that no beneficial sparse ablation exists. The theory (one-layer 3-head diagonal softmax attention, two conflicting tasks, small Gaussian init, full-batch gradient descent) shows that with probability at least 4/9 a head carrying the conflicting feature can be removed to cut task A risk to 0 while raising task B risk from t^2 to 4t^2, and the paper states it does not establish that this mechanism explains the gains in the real language models. Ablation gain here is a task-conflict effect between tasks, not a measure of how much capability a component carries.
the stability of the selected subsets and their gains across different discovery samples remains insufficiently characterized.
Section 4.2-4.4, Theorem 4.2 and 4.3, pp. 7-9

Theory finding relevant to localization: in the toy model the jointly optimal predictor is fixed but its split across heads is not, and gradient descent from small random initialization concentrates each feature in one head (off-winner coefficients of order alpha^4). Each task has risk a^2/4 at the joint optimum, and removing the head that holds the conflicting feature improves one task while worsening the other. Implication: a small component can look like it carries a capability gain or a loss only relative to a chosen task mix; a localization claim must report the effect on the other tasks, not only the target. Theory only, simplified model, not tested on RL.
Joint optimization therefore selects w⋆ 0 = a/2, while fitting the task-specific coefficients (b) and (c) exactly.

papers.title: Neural Networks Are Already Clean
f: The Short Version

Preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B MLP neurons (agent-written neuron papers, positive and negative pole counted separately): about 90% of neuron poles have one main job, about 7% two related jobs, 2-4% not understood; GPT-2 XL re-audit on 500 neurons gives about 70%. The number is a rough estimate that depends on the weak-activation threshold; no benchmark intervention is behind it.
roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job
Exploring Language Models (double-negative SwiGLU)

SwiGLU double-negative regime (gate<0 and value<0 gives a positive output): for about 4% of Qwen3-32B neurons this leak is the whole top-k list. Ablating these across the whole network raises most benchmarks but lowers some reasoning ones (no benchmark names or numbers given; authors guess some neuron uses the leak to reason longer). Read neurons with the four gate/value sign regimes separated.
Ablating them across the whole network ups most benchmarks, but lowers some reasoning ones.
Exploring Language Models (negative poles, Santa graph)

Negative poles carry behaviour that top-k positive labels miss: in Qwen3-32B, ablating 8 neurons whose negative pole is Santa drops P(Santa) from 0.997 (random same-layer ablation) to 0.059, while ablating the 20 neurons labelled Christmas/Santa by positive top-k only drops it to 76%. Select neurons by attribution to the output and read both poles, not by label.
Remove the eight neurons with a Santa negative side and Santa falls from near-certain to 6%
Appendix: Memorization and Composition

Clamping intervention in Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: zeroing every neuron output whenever its gate exceeds its ordinary-text 99.9th percentile breaks recitation (Psalm 23 denied, then the model repeats a phrase to the 400-token limit, i.e. it induces a repetition loop); count- or magnitude-matched random interventions keep the verse; some arithmetic and summarization still work, coding degrades. One saved experiment, no benchmark number.
ordinary-text 99.9th percentile, recitation can fall apart
Do Weak Activations Matter?

Strong activations carry the function: of 100 million tokens through one Qwen3-32B neuron about 160 reach the strong half (above half of max). In a 7.06M ConvNeXt, removing the weakest 75% of activations in all 18 blocks moves ImageNet accuracy 72% to 71%, removing the strongest 7% (same total activation) moves it 72% to 4%. In language models the place where weak activations cost most is the last layer, which suppresses single tokens.
Almost all sit near zero; about 160 reach the strong half.

papers.title: Adaptive Nucleus Truncation for Long-Form Reasoning
f: Sec. 2-3, Eq. 1 and 4, p. 3

ANTS: top-n-sigma truncation in logit space, width n_t = n0 + gamma*H(p at T=1), gamma chosen per prompt by a Thompson bandit (gamma 5-32, 10 arms, plus a no-truncation arm) rewarded by entropy. Direction: confident (low-H) positions are truncated hardest, high-H positions keep more tokens. This is the opposite of 'keep the tail at confident positions'. Temperature itself is constant.
High-entropy contexts therefore retain more alternatives, while low-entropy contexts are pruned more sharply
Sec. 4, p. 4-5; Table 1, p. 5

ANTS is used for RL rollouts on a 33B-total/4B-active MoE; gains are averaged over RL checkpoints vs a no-truncation sampler, so sampler and training effects are mixed.
